title: Hōkūleʻa: supported voyaging and inter-island renewal
summary: A modern voyaging programme combined a reconstructed canoe, living Micronesian instruction, Hawaiian purposes and research infrastructure. Operational success and formal transmission are documented; prehistoric route reconstruction and general cultural causation remain separate questions.

stages.invention: No first-invention claim; canoe and navigation practices drew on multiple bodies of knowledge.
stages.feasibility: 1976 and 1980 voyages; 1980 participant record explicitly describes supported non-instrument navigation.
stages.deployment: Repeated staffed voyages, later pupils and March 2007 initiation.
stages.diffusion: Named canoes and pupils provide qualitative spread within a network; no population denominator.
stages.displacement/reversal: 1978 capsize interrupted the programme; 1980 voyage followed. No commercial displacement claim.

counterevidence: Support craft and modern training matter; PVS commemorative accounts are not independent impact evaluations. Women’s accounts complicate a solely male-master narrative.

episode.technology_configuration: Hōkūleʻa programme: double-hulled sailing canoe, skilled non-instrument navigator, trained crew, research/escort supports; 2007 Pwo transmission is a later subepisode.
episode.task: Make planned ocean landfalls and renew knowledge, responsibility and collective identity.
episode.population: Named PVS voyage crews and navigators; later eleven Satawal and five Hawaiʻi initiates; purposively interviewed women voyagers are a separate qualitative sample.
episode.interval: 1976–1980 operational sequence; 1979–2007 transmission sequence; women interviewed by 2010, including a dated 2007 interview.
contemporary_alternatives: Instrument-assisted sailing and modern marine transport, available for transport but not equivalent to the cultural/learning task
Not joining or discontinuing the voluntary programme; individual opportunity costs incompletely recorded
episode.adoption_measure: Recorded voyages, named pupils and a specific initiation cohort; no share of Pacific navigators, crews or households.
episode.observation_limits: Survivor/commemoration bias; formal recognition is not a standardized proficiency denominator; no ancient-voyage uptake inferred.

actors.chooser: Mau chose to teach; learners and PVS organized participation; interviewed women explain their own purposes.
actors.payer: PVS and supporting institutions supplied canoe/programme resources; full finance and donor allocation not inspected; volunteers supplied time.
actors.operator_maintainer: Navigators, crews, canoe builders and volunteers; named teaching and voyage roles observed, maintenance payroll unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Families bearing time commitments and communities represented by voyages; distribution not measured.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Mau’s agreement and women’s voluntary time are documented; some interviewees withheld genealogy. Crew access and gendered selection rules are not established.

labour.tasks: Navigation, weather/sea observation, crew coordination, teaching, canoe work and volunteering; wages largely unobserved.
labour.entry_barriers: Hundreds of hours of preparation in the 1980 account, sea experience, access to teachers and capacity to volunteer; neither universal equality nor a quantified gender barrier is established.
labour.bargaining_ownership: PVS organizes vessels; teachers control transmission and recognition; no complete ownership or decision-rights audit.
labour.transition: Named learner Nainoa trained before 1980; later 2007 initiates show cohort transmission, not cohort wage mobility.
labour.distribution: Women’s accounts establish participation and purposes; no comparative income or opportunity distribution.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot estimate jobs created, returns to credentials, household costs or safety rates.

title: Gunditjmara Tae Rak: hydraulic modification, disabling and negotiated restoration
period: c.6600 cal BP–present archaeological context; restoration episode 1954–2010
summary: A dated feature demonstrates changing trap construction. The modern episode tracks pastoral drainage, a failed restoration trial, land return and a negotiated weir, without assuming uninterrupted ancient operation or restored historic output.

stages.invention: Unknown; c.6600 cal BP dates concern one channel sequence, not invention of aquaculture.
stages.deployment: Material channels/walls and documented fishery; modern portable nets/traps persisted alongside changing hydraulics.
stages.diffusion: Regional complexes known but no dated adopter/area denominator.
stages.displacement/reversal: 1954 drainage sharply restricted functioning; opposed by Gunditjmara Elders according to dossier.
stages.feasibility: Modern hydrological studies and failed trial precede 2010 completed weir.
stages.scaling: No inferred aquaculture production scale from mapped stonework or restored water alone.

counterevidence: Sources on restoration share a project lineage. Increased retained water is distinct from observed operation of every trap and from historical livelihood restoration.

episode.technology_configuration: Ancient comparator: F10 channel and later walls at Muldoons. Main modern episode: Tae Rak drainage, regulator/weir and compatible trap elevations.
episode.task: Capture/hold fish, especially kooyang; restore cultural water landscape while limiting impacts on upstream farms.
episode.population: Ancient builders/operators at one feature, numerically unknown; modern Gunditjmara restoration institutions, local workers and neighboring landholders are a separate observed population.
episode.interval: Channel c.6600 cal BP and later walls c.600–800 cal BP; drainage completed 1954; proposals/trials from 1970s–1980s; construction January–May 2010.
contemporary_alternatives: Portable nets and traps documented as continuing fishing methods
Drainage and pastoral use favored by some landholders
Earlier trial weir, documented as unsuccessful
Higher lake-water restoration constrained by adjacent property effects
episode.adoption_measure: Stratified site evidence and completed project chronology; 52.4 m AHD design setting; no catch, fishery-user or worker denominator.
episode.observation_limits: Mixed epochs are kept separate; archaeological survival does not prove continuous use; hydraulic availability does not count operating traps.

actors.chooser: Ancient decision structure unknown; modern Gunditjmara advocated restoration, agencies authorized works and adjoining owners influenced feasible water level.
actors.payer: Modern Indigenous Land Corporation planning funding and state construction resources; federal employment support reported; ancient labor/resource contributions unknown.
actors.operator_maintainer: Gunditjmara fishers; restoration designers, contractors and trained Indigenous construction workers; ongoing staffing not quantified.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Gunditjmara users affected by imposed drainage; upstream farmers affected by retained water; ecology and downstream uses.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Dossier records objections to drainage that did not stop it. Restoration required consultation and negotiated constraint; no assumption of equal vetoes.

labour.tasks: Channel/wall/trap building and upkeep inferred from features; modern design, construction, administration and training documented.
labour.entry_barriers: Land/water access, ecological and construction knowledge; modern tasks used on-site training and supervision. Ancient apprenticeship and exclusion rules unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ancient tenure not established; return of lake to Gunditjmara in March 2008 changed control before construction, but neighboring property interests continued to constrain level.
labour.transition: 1954 loss of operating water followed by decades of proposals; 2010 construction jobs documented, not longitudinal worker careers.
labour.distribution: Specific Indigenous participation in construction reported; no pay, retention or household-benefit breakdown.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer egalitarian ancient aquaculture, total fish output, restoration profitability or sustained employment.

title: Martu hunting fires and localized mosaic maintenance
region: Western Desert, Western Australia; Great and Little Sandy Desert bioregions
summary: Skilled burning accompanied small-game hunting in a mixed contemporary economy. Comparative landscape data support a local fuel-mosaic mechanism, while observed benefits and motives remain distinct.

stages.deployment: Directly observed hunting and ignition practices, with vehicle access and store purchases.
stages.diffusion: No adoption-rate estimate; spatial concentration around community tracks is measured exposure/use.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Fire use varies by prey, task, season and distance; remote comparison zones mainly lightning-driven.
stages.scaling: Effects are strongest at forager-day-range scale; no uniform continental effect inferred.

counterevidence: Observed hunting choices are not randomized. Climate and topography matter, roads proxy access, and fire-age heterogeneity is not a complete measure of biodiversity.

episode.technology_configuration: Martu cool-season patch burning in spinifex for small burrowed game; vehicle trips to camps followed by foot foraging.
episode.task: Acquire food and manage familiar Country through skilled practices; some ecological effects may accompany rather than exhaust stated purposes.
episode.population: 2008 study: 421 bouts/59 camp-days in 2002; 2012 study: 104 foragers and 1,811 bouts across 347 sampled days, not all Martu people.
episode.interval: 1999–2010 remote imagery; 2000–2010 foraging programme with focused 2002 study.
contemporary_alternatives: Hunt different prey or collect plants
Purchase store food; not a complete substitute for social and cultural purposes
Lightning-driven burning in less-accessed comparison landscapes
episode.adoption_measure: Recorded behavior by hunting bout and task; fire-regime zones near tracks/communities versus remote zones; no total household denominator.
episode.observation_limits: The 2012 regime classes cover 10% and 50% of the study region respectively, leaving other/mixed areas outside these categories; sampled fieldwork and spatial proxies limit inference.

actors.chooser: Individual foragers and groups choose tasks/patches within customary rights; S08 describes potential retribution for burning areas without rights and social value in caring for Country.
actors.payer: Foragers supply labor and contemporary transport resources; program-level subsidies/funding not analyzed.
actors.operator_maintainer: Primarily women in observed small-game burning; men’s task mix includes other hunting and some patch burning; practices recur through ordinary foraging.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other users, households receiving food and organisms affected by fire; S08 describes burning unharvested resources as a social cost.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Variation between burning and non-burning hunts indicates task-level discretion, within land rights and obligations; enforcement prevalence and equal access are not audited.

labour.tasks: Hunting, ignition, tracking, digging, processing, sharing and travel; ecological maintenance overlaps subsistence rather than appearing as a separate paid occupation.
labour.entry_barriers: Experienced ecological reading, knowledge of land, mobility and access to vehicles/tracks; age/skill and asset distributions not fully quantified.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Martu are Traditional Owners; sources measure foraging and ecology, not detailed control over land-management payments or household bargaining.
labour.transition: Outstation return in 1980s is background; studied 2000s practices combine purchased goods with foraging. No individual employment transitions.
labour.distribution: Gender differences in tasks are observed; edible-energy returns are not money or household welfare. No class/age income estimates.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot estimate paid ranger employment, carbon revenues, net welfare or ancient labor systems.

title: Kuk Phase 3 drainage: variable use and unresolved abandonment
region: Wahgi Valley, Papua New Guinea; comparator highland valleys
period: c.4350–2500 cal BP Phase 3; c.2000 cal BP Phase 4 resumption
summary: Ditch networks at Kuk extend earlier cultivation configurations but are neither a linear intensification curve nor an archaeological transcript of social organization. Wetland use ceased before a later configuration emerged; reasons remain unresolved.

stages.invention: Origins and immediate motivations not established; chronology alone is not proof of independent invention.
stages.deployment: Ditch networks and maintenance traces demonstrate local modification for cultivation, interpreted jointly with environmental evidence.
stages.diffusion: Other valleys have dated ditches but thinner sampling; no direction or rate of transfer inferred.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Wetter northern portions appear undrained; dryland gardening was another option.
stages.displacement/reversal: Several-hundred-year Phase 3–4 gap before later grid systems; no demonstrated total knowledge loss.

counterevidence: Hydrological, agronomic and social explanations can fit the same surviving sequence; modern property analogies cannot fill absent ancient institutional data.

episode.technology_configuration: Phase 3 rectilinear, dendritic and other ditch arrangements at Kuk wetland margins; Phase 2 mounds and Phase 4 grids are distinct comparators.
episode.task: Drain cultivation surfaces; possible boundary/risk functions remain hypotheses.
episode.population: Users/builders of excavated Kuk fields, population and household counts unknown; other valley sites are limited comparators.
episode.interval: Phase 3 starts c.4350–3980 cal BP; later stage c.2700–2500 years ago; Phase 4 begins around 2000 years ago. Dates approximate, BP convention anchored to 1950 where calibrated.
contemporary_alternatives: Hunting/gathering and mixed land-use portfolios, quantities unknown
episode.adoption_measure: Dated stratigraphic features, plan extent and different networks; no operator, hectare-use or production denominator through time.
episode.observation_limits: Wetland channels preserve differently from dryland practice; resolution cannot establish every continuous interval or simultaneous regional abandonment.

actors.chooser: Ancient individuals/groups unknown; do not infer chiefs or state command from ditch scale.
actors.payer: Labor/material providers unknown; manual earthmoving evident but contribution rules unrecorded.
actors.operator_maintainer: Diggers and cultivators; maintenance represented by tools/features, demographic identities unknown.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Other water/land users plausibly affected, but impact and status not recoverable from selected sources.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Unknown: no direct evidence of work obligations, displacement or voluntary abandonment for this episode.

labour.tasks: Excavation, cleaning/repair, planting, harvesting and fallowing; labor quantities and paid/unpaid categories cannot be reconstructed reliably.
labour.entry_barriers: Land access and cultivation/drainage skills plausible requirements; actual allocation, exclusion and training unknown.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Ditches may mark tenure, but control of land and output remains an interpretation rather than documented rights.
labour.transition: Long material sequence with discontinuity; no individual or cohort career evidence.
labour.distribution: No defensible household, gender or status distribution of gains.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer egalitarianism, coerced labor, occupational specialization or livelihood improvement from landscape investment.

title: Māori kūmara: local adaptation, experimental limits and knowledge recovery
region: M24/11, Mohua/Golden Bay, Aotearoa New Zealand
Robin Hood Bay and Whatarangi, Cook Strait
period: Fourteenth–eighteenth-century archaeological contexts; trials 1999–2002; Pōhatu study published 2025
summary: Separate site and research episodes show crop cultivation, experimental feasibility and collaborative reconstruction. They are compared as distinct evidence, not merged into one uninterrupted tradition or regional adoption rate.

stages.invention: No first introduction or independent invention claim.
stages.deployment: M24/11 and Pōhatu modified soils and crop evidence support historical gardening at those localities.
stages.feasibility: Cook Strait trials demonstrate selected cultivars growing under modern conditions; not ancient yields.
stages.diffusion: Local remains and cultivar histories do not supply a regional diffusion denominator.
stages.non-adoption/niche: Different crops/sites face different climates; absence of remains does not establish universal rejection.
stages.displacement/reversal: Pōhatu land alienation/disconnection documented through community-linked scholarship; contemporary garden re-establishment is a goal, not a measured outcome.

counterevidence: Starch identifications and ancient fertilizer interpretations are uncertain. Trials have modern confounders. Distinct locations, climates and users cannot be pooled into a historical yield or adoption estimate.

episode.technology_configuration: Three explicit subepisodes: A, M24/11 archaeological cultivation surfaces and probable crop microremains; B, experimental Cook Strait gardens using returned collection cultivars; C, Pōhatu modified-soil investigation guided by Mana Whenua knowledge.
episode.task: A: grow foods in local conditions; B: investigate possible growth and labor/yield constraints; C: recover cultivation history and support desired reconnection.
episode.population: A: historical site cultivators, counts/identities unresolved; B: modern research gardeners with iwi consultation; C: Te Rūnaka o Koukourārata Mana Whenua and research partners. These populations are not interchangeable.
episode.interval: A: fourteenth-century and post-1650 contexts; B: 1999–2002 observations published 2003; C: historical precolonial/early colonial gardening context, contemporary study published 2025.
contemporary_alternatives: Historical other introduced crops, native food plants and aquatic/animal resources; their shares unknown
Different soils, crop varieties, planting times and storage practices
Modern laboratory soil analysis and community knowledge used together, not mutually exclusive alternatives
episode.adoption_measure: Site microremains and modified soils; separate experimental plot harvests; research workflow and stated restoration aims. No combined farmer/household adoption measure.
episode.observation_limits: Experimental yields do not measure historical diffusion; site sampling cannot prove crop extinction; collaborative research is not completed commercial or subsistence restoration.

actors.chooser: A: ancient garden decision-makers unresolved; B: researchers with consultation/support from named iwi authorities; C: Mana Whenua helped frame questions and interpretations.
actors.payer: A: unknown labor contributors; B/C: research resources and land access, complete budgets uninspected.
actors.operator_maintainer: A: gardeners maintaining soil, planting stocks and stores; B: experimental gardeners; C: knowledge holders and researchers. Ancient gender division unestablished.
actors.affected_nonchooser: Historical communities affected by land transfer; landholders and descendants in contemporary research; no full impact measurement.
actors.ability_to_refuse: Pōhatu historical displacement limits choice; modern iwi consultation and access permission documented. Historical crop selection cannot be read as fully unconstrained preference.

labour.tasks: Soil amendment, mound preparation, planting, weeding, storage; research sampling, interpretation and knowledge transmission are later distinct tasks.
labour.entry_barriers: Suitable land/microclimate, viable planting stock, storage skill and knowledge access; trial windbreaks/treated stock change entry requirements.
labour.bargaining_ownership: Pōhatu’s alienation/private ownership interrupted direct access; current research recognises Mana Whenua authority but is not a documented land restitution.
labour.transition: No tracked ancient household transitions or contemporary paid-work cohort. Plant collection’s repatriation/treatment is observed but not equivalent to restoration of all local cultivars.
labour.distribution: No income/wage distribution; scientific knowledge recovery is an observed process, food sovereignty an expressed purpose.
labour.evidence_limit: Cannot infer ancient surplus per worker, gender equality, exact crop portfolios or successful new livelihoods from these different evidence streams.
